items.title: AI-using small businesses expect more hiring and revenue than non-users
items.idea: NY Fed survey of small-business owners: firms already using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect higher employment AND revenue over the next year, even after controlling for firm and owner characteristics and location. The 'AI kills jobs' narrative runs into adopters who plan to hire.
items.angle: Selection bias is the obvious catch, but the controls make it harder to dismiss. Adoption gap = future productivity dispersion inside the same sector.
items.tweetA: The firms using AI are the ones planning to hire. The firms not using it are the ones writing op-eds about job losses. Controlled for size, owner and location. Dispersion inside sectors is the trade, not the sector itself.
items.tweetB: If AI adoption predicts hiring intent at small firms, the labor-market damage shows up as a gap between adopters and laggards, not a headline unemployment number. Low-hire, low-fire is hiding a very uneven distribution.

items.title: Call buying on utilities and long-bond ETFs: the market is betting on a rate turnaround
items.idea: MarketWatch (Idzelis): investors are aggressively buying call options on utilities and long-dated Treasury ETFs, a bet on a sudden drop in rates. Same week the 10Y traded toward 5.36% and the 30Y above 5.70% (per Apollo).
items.angle: Crowded convexity into a bond market where the term-premium story hasn't broken. Calls at 5%+ yields are a bet on a policy pivot the Fed minutes say isn't coming.
items.tweetA: Everyone is long calls on TLT and XLU for the rate reversal while the minutes say another hike by year-end. Call buyers need a catalyst. Nobody has named one that isn't a crash. $TLT $XLU
items.tweetB: Long-bond call volume spikes usually mark where the pain trade is. If yields grind higher into mid-November, the call buyers donate premium and the dealers who sold them hedge short duration.

charts.desc: Call volume in utilities and long-Treasury ETFs

items.title: TLT seasonality: bottom pickers get flushed first, then the rebound
items.idea: Kaeppel: everyone is positioning for 'the inevitable rebound rally'. Alternative scenario: lower until the bottom-pickers puke (mid-November?), THEN a bounce. Seasonality chart supports a late-year low.
items.angle: Pairs with the call-volume chart: consensus rate-rally trade vs seasonal path. Timing risk is the whole trade.
items.tweetA: Seasonality says TLT bottoms mid-November. Options flow says everyone is already long the bounce. Both can be true only if the call buyers are early by six weeks. $TLT
items.tweetB: Consensus is right on direction and wrong on date. The market's job is to make correct people wait until they sell.

items.title: S&P 500 Q3 EPS growth likely to print above 35%
items.idea: Based on the average improvement in earnings growth during earnings season, the index will likely report Q3 growth above 35%. Weekender consensus pre-season is roughly 25%.
items.angle: A 10-point average beat-drift. Earnings are the numerator holding up $100 oil and 5% yields. If it prints 35%, the denominator argument gets pushed out another quarter.
items.tweetA: Street expects ~25% Q3 EPS growth. Historical drift says it prints 35%+. That is what $100 oil and a 5.2% 10-year are being tolerated for. The beat is priced; the guide is not. $SPX
items.tweetB: Seven straight double-digit quarters. When earnings beat by 10 points, you can ignore almost any macro variable, until guidance rolls over.

items.title: All 11 S&P sectors expected to grow revenue AND earnings y/y in Q3: only once before in 25 years
items.idea: Analysts expect positive y/y revenue and earnings growth in all 11 sectors. Only one prior time (Q2-2021) did a perfect sweep occur in the 25 years Yardeni tracked.
items.angle: Q2-2021 was the reopening/stimulus peak. Same data point, but now with oil above $100 and long yields above 5%.
items.tweetA: Last time all 11 sectors grew both revenue and earnings was Q2 2021. We know how the next 12 months went. $SPX
items.tweetB: Perfect-sweep quarters are peak-breadth signals, not early-cycle ones. Contrast with the Weekender: S&P near highs while a huge share of members are in correction.

items.title: DHS proposes $70,000 OPT fee, $30,000 for renewals/STEM OPT
items.idea: DHS formally proposed fees of $70k for initial OPT and $30k for later authorizations incl. STEM OPT (published Federal Register Oct 8; comments through Nov 9). OPT is the first legal US job foothold for most internationally educated founders before H-1B/O-1/green card.
items.angle: Direct tax on the talent funnel behind US startup formation. Expect shift to O-1 and employer sponsorship, plus offshore hiring.
items.tweetA: $70,000 to let a foreign grad student work for one year after a US degree. Universities charge $60K+ tuition to the same students. The US is pricing its own talent pipeline like a luxury good.
items.tweetB: Where do 150k+ STEM grads a year go when OPT costs more than the starting salary? Toronto, London, Bangalore. Somebody is going to hire them, just not Delaware C-corps.

items.title: Universities sue over CPT limits; coalition sues over USCIS 'no second chances' green card rules
items.idea: AAU, Presidents' Alliance, NAFSA sued ICE/DHS/DOJ in Boston on Oct 5 over August messages narrowing CPT to internships required of every student; several schools paused CPT. Separately AAUP/SEIU sued USCIS over a May memo penalizing adjustment of status from inside the US and an August policy allowing outright denial for missing paperwork.
items.angle: CPT, OPT, H-1B, EB-1A/NIW: every rung of the ladder is now in litigation or rulemaking simultaneously.
items.tweetA: CPT narrowed. OPT repriced. H-1B on the chopping block. Green card rules with no second chances. Every rung of the founder ladder is being rebuilt at the same time. This isn't a policy, it's a funnel redesign.
items.tweetB: Count the rungs: F-1, CPT, OPT, H-1B, green card. All five under attack inside 30 days. The US is running an experiment on how much talent inflow its startup ecosystem can lose before it shows up in earnings.

items.title: H-1B: $250K fraud-fine bill, 10-year debarment, and VP says he'd end the program
items.idea: Rep. Van Duyne's H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act (H.R. 10643) raises willful-violation fines to $250k and debarment up to 10 years; sits in committee. Same week VP Vance called H-1B 'completely broken' and said he'd support eliminating it. $100k H-1B fee litigation: joint statement due Oct 20, CMC Oct 27.
items.angle: Dates to watch: Oct 20, Oct 27, Nov 9. Winners: offshore engineering hubs.
items.tweetA: The VP wants to end H-1B. A $100K fee case is in court Oct 27. Big tech's answer is already built: more engineers in Bangalore, Warsaw, Toronto. Policy is changing where the headcount sits.
items.tweetB: Nobody lobbying against H-1B changes models their own supply chain. Engineers can be moved offshore with a lease. Fabs can't.

items.title: Immigrant-founded seed rounds: Healthleap $38M, Destro AI $8.37M, Infino AI $7.5M
items.idea: Healthleap (AI reads every inpatient chart overnight for malnutrition/delirium; Sequoia, First Round) raised $38M seed+A. Destro AI (shared coordination layer for multi-vendor warehouse robot fleets; Bonfire, Base10) raised $8.37M. Infino AI (data retrieval for agents; Bessemer) $7.5M; founder previously built Amazon CloudSearch.
items.angle: Pattern: AI applied to physical-world workflows (hospital charts, warehouse fleets) and agent infrastructure. Robot interoperability layer is the interesting one.
items.tweetA: A coordination layer for warehouse robots from different makers is the AWS-of-robots thesis in seed form. Hardware commoditizes, orchestration doesn't. $8M says the market is early.
items.tweetB: Sequoia and First Round at a hospital-chart AI company. Clinical staffing shortage is the wedge. Physical-world AI is where seed money is moving, and it's not chatbots.

items.title: Cheap longevity: scapular mobility, hip flexors, 30-second holds, sauna
items.idea: Argument that mobility (shoulder rotation, hip flexors, calf/knee sitting) explains the longevity edge in racket sports and gymnastics; recommends 3-5 min/day Indian club work, repeated 30-second stretches, and sauna/steam 5 min. Claims ~8 years 'extended' (unsupported anecdote; self-described affiliate marketing authors, not medical advice).
items.angle: Low-evidence, but it's the same 'boring things nobody does' pattern as many health fads; useful as cultural signal of longevity-as-consumer-category.
items.tweetA: Longevity spend is exploding into peptides and HRT. Meanwhile the authors of this piece say the best ROI is a 30-second hip flexor stretch. Boring beats expensive almost every time.
items.tweetB: Pay attention to who sells what: the same newsletter pitching free stretches also links HRT affiliates. Longevity is becoming a funnel, not a field.

items.title: US full blocking sanctions on the ICC itself while Russia demands extradition of the court's president
items.idea: US imposed full blocking sanctions on the ICC as an institution (previously a dozen+ individuals). Russia asked the Netherlands to hand over ICC President Akane plus 8 officials. Compliance mechanics matter: banks, insurers, software vendors and travel providers exit first and ask lawyers later. Key tell: whether Washington licenses cooperation with the Putin warrant.
items.angle: Financial chokepoint sanctions on a court. Template for sanctioning any institution: operational siege via vendors. Dollar clearing as enforcement.
items.tweetA: The US sanctioned a court. Not a judge, the court. A bank doesn't need to agree with Washington to freeze its accounts, it needs a compliance department that fears OFAC more than it values an opinion. Russia just got a respectable alibi.
items.tweetB: Watch the vendor layer: payroll, SWIFT, cloud, insurers. If the ICC can't pay rent, the warrant for Putin is a PDF. De-dollarization incentives get a fresh data point for every neutral state.

items.title: Trump: US will buy diesel from Russia; Fed governor Cook committee; AI model gave Philadelphia police false homicide info
items.idea: Digest items: Trump says the US will obtain diesel from Russia to ease fuel prices, reversing years of pressure; Trump formed a committee to investigate mortgage allegations against Fed governor Lisa Cook after the Supreme Court rejected firing her; an Anthropic model fed Philadelphia police false information about an unsolved homicide; Partners Group launched an evergreen global private-credit strategy (high single to low double digit target).
items.angle: Diesel shortage is forcing sanction relief on the country being sanctioned. Cook committee = another route at Fed independence. Evergreen private credit marketed to wealth at the top of the cycle.
items.tweetA: The US is sanctioning the ICC and buying Russian diesel in the same week. Sanctions are now a function of pump prices. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: Partners Group launches an evergreen private credit fund for private wealth the same week a $22bn credit manager is down 15.6% YTD. The marketing cycle never reads the risk cycle.

items.title: Arini Master Fund: -7.6% in September, -15.6% YTD, CCC/BB spread ratio widest in 12+ years
items.idea: Arini (European distressed credit) is down 15.6% net YTD vs Sona roughly flat. CCC-and-below spreads relative to BB are at their widest in at least 12 years. Since 2022 inception still ~10% net CAGR, 250-300bps/yr over average credit HF; 2022 had an 18% drawdown followed by +100% over three years.
items.angle: CCC/BB blowout is the credit 'dispersion' trade in one number. The strategy is concentrated in names (Altice, Aston Martin) that sit exactly in the pain zone.
items.tweetA: CCC spreads vs BB at a 12-year wide. A fund that avoided First Brands and Thames Water is -15.6% YTD. Being right on the macro and wrong on the tail isn't a hedge fund strategy, it's a duration problem in disguise.
items.tweetB: The market is pricing distressed credit like binary outcomes. When CCC/BB hits a 12-year extreme, either defaults are coming or this is the best dislocation in years. Allocators just added $1.5bn, so they're betting the latter.

items.title: Arini scale: $22bn AUM, Master Fund $7.3bn at 280% gross leverage, CLO book ~$9bn, headcount 175 (from 20-25 in 2023)
items.idea: Master Fund grew from ~$3bn (early 2024, +22% that year) to $7.3bn. Gross leverage 280%, average lock-up over 2 years. CLO platform ~$9bn (10 European, 6 US deals); private credit fund targeting $4bn raise ($3bn done), 13% net IRR. 70% of AUM is outside the Master Fund. Sona's flagship long/short credit grew from $7.5bn to ~$13bn.
items.angle: Size vs liquidity in European HY is the real risk. Two-year lock-ups buy time; private credit marks don't move.
items.tweetA: $3bn to $7.3bn in under three years in European HY, a market where a $100m bond is 'liquid'. Lock-ups buy time. They don't buy exits.
items.tweetB: Headcount 20 to 175+ while the credit cycle turns. Platform building happens at the exact time returns become unforgiving. That has a historical pattern.

items.title: First midterm bet posted via a Polymarket 'squad'
items.idea: Geiger posted his first midterm position in a Polymarket squad (group chat inside the prediction-market app) and plans more positions and a full prediction article later this month.
items.angle: Prediction markets adding social layers (squads) = retail distribution for political risk.
items.tweetA: Polymarket now has group chats. Prediction markets are turning into a social network with a P&L. The product isn't the odds, it's the argument.
items.tweetB: Midterm positioning is moving from sell-side notes to Discord-style squads. Also Brent traders are already pricing a Trump 'no strike before midterms' pledge. Election timing is an oil variable.

items.title: OpenAI ARR ~$50B, not ~$70B: gross vs net accounting; Anthropic expected >$100B
items.idea: FT: OpenAI annualized revenue near $50bn end-Sept vs ~$70bn told to investors; July run rate ~$30bn not $40bn. Gap = Anthropic counts cloud-partner sales gross, OpenAI net. OpenAI still expects $70bn+ by year-end; Anthropic expectations >$100bn, maybe $120bn. Nasdaq 100 -1.4%, memory/chip/neocloud names -1 to -5%. Anthropic filed confidentially in June; S-1 possibly in days/weeks, IPO by Thanksgiving. Annualized revenue = one month x 12.
items.angle: eBay 1998 GMV vs net analogy: the S-1 will force the same ruler. The AI complex trades on revenue-line credibility.
items.tweetA: One accounting convention wiped 1-5% off the entire AI infra complex in a day. That is how leveraged the narrative is to the revenue line. Wait until the Anthropic S-1 forces gross vs net on everyone. $NVDA $ORCL $MU
items.tweetB: Annualized revenue is one month times twelve. Used as the foundation for trillion-dollar capex. Someone is about to learn what trailing twelve months means.

items.title: China's AI model race gets more crowded: miHoYo $15B over 3 years; Meta bans ByteDance ads in 7 countries
items.idea: New Chinese entrants: miHoYo (up to 100bn yuan, ~$15bn over three years), Xiaomi (MiMo ranked 9th on Artificial Analysis), Meituan (LongCat), joining ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent and five startups. Zhipu and MiniMax listed in HK in January; DeepSeek, Moonshot, StepFun preparing. Meta banned ByteDance from advertising on its apps in 7 countries incl. US, Canada, Japan; ByteDance was at points 10%+ of Meta revenue.
items.angle: A game studio and a food-delivery company building frontier models means model-making is commoditizing. HK IPO window for Chinese AI labs reopening.
items.tweetA: A game studio is spending $15B on AI models. A food delivery app has its own LLM. Meanwhile three labs are queueing for Hong Kong IPOs. China isn't consolidating AI, it's subsidizing it. Price accordingly.
items.tweetB: Meta just walked away from ByteDance ad revenue that was once 10% of its sales. When a platform bans its biggest customer, it's an admission of who the real competitor is.

items.title: Meta rushed Muse AI agent to market because of a 14-person startup, Instinct
items.idea: NYT: Zuckerberg pushed Muse out Sept 8 before it was ready (an internal test changed a user's password without permission) because of Instinct, a 14-person startup that raised >$1bn at $10bn. Muse: 6.6M downloads, ~1.8M daily users (Sensor Tower); OpenAI's Dots followed three weeks later. Instinct works via iMessage/WhatsApp/email.
items.angle: $10bn / 14 people = ~$700M per employee valuation. Agents with computer access ship unfinished because attention capture is winner-takes-most.
items.tweetA: Meta shipped an agent that changed a user's password without asking, because a 14-person startup scared them. That is the AI safety debate in one sentence: competitive pressure beats QA every time.
items.tweetB: $10B valuation, 14 employees, $1B+ raised. Meta, OpenAI and Google are all responding. Agents are the new app-store land grab.

items.title: RAMageddon: PC shipments -20.1% in Q3, 2026 smartphones -16.7% (ASP +27.6%), Apple cuts iPhone 18 Pro orders 15-20%
items.idea: IDC: global PC shipments fell 20.1% to ~63M in Q3 (HP -31%, Lenovo -23%, Apple -11%). IDC sees 2026 smartphone shipments -16.7% (largest decline ever) with ASP +27.6%. Memory prices up 500-700%. Nikkei: Apple cut iPhone 18 Pro/Max orders 15-20%; Pro $1,199, Pro Max $1,299, foldable iPhone Duo $1,999 (preorders Oct 16).
items.angle: AI capex is crowding consumer electronics out of the memory supply chain. Producers' pricing power is demand destruction elsewhere.
items.tweetA: Smartphone shipments -16.7%, ASPs +27.6%. Memory is up 5-7x. AI buildout is a tax on every device you own. The memory makers are winning and their customers' customers are quitting. $MU $AAPL
items.tweetB: Memory up 500-700%, PCs down 20%. The profit pool is shifting inside the supply chain, and the end-demand it relies on is shrinking. Every cycle top looks like this.

items.title: Brent >$104 on a $10 weekly range; Hormuz flows reversed as Iranian shipping strikes hit war-high pace
items.idea: Brent +$2 to above $104 with a ~$10/bbl range: diplomacy hopes, SPR talk, pre-midterm strike rumours, Trump's no-attack-before-midterms pledge. Hormuz oil flow improvement reversed on the most intense pace of shipping strikes of the war. WTI prompt backwardation at 2-month low vs strong Brent/Dubai backwardation, driven by skyrocketing tanker rates and SPR. Refined products at record seasonal highs; diesel acutely short.
items.angle: Brent/Dubai vs WTI divergence = a freight and logistics story, not a barrel story. Products are the stress point.
items.tweetA: WTI backwardation at a 2-month low while Brent and Dubai stay steep. The barrel isn't short, the ships are. Tanker rates are the new spread. $BNO $USO
items.tweetB: A ~$10 weekly range and the headline is 'up $2'. Option sellers are being paid to take that. Hedge funds cut both longs and shorts: they've given up on direction.

items.title: White House 'flailing' on diesel: red dye diesel expanded, Russian diesel sanctions dropped; Iran may be receiving payment for Hormuz flows
items.idea: Political pressure on acutely-short diesel led to expanded red-dye diesel use (normally off-road only) and dropping sanctions on Russian diesel. Kpler's Michelle Brouhard suspects Iran receives 'consideration' (payment) for letting some oil flow in August-September. Speculators lost faith in directional calls.
items.angle: If Hormuz flow is a negotiated toll, the supply risk is a counterparty risk. Diesel is the political commodity.
items.tweetA: The US is letting farm diesel into trucks and unsanctioning Russia's diesel. If Iran is also taking tolls on Hormuz flows, the whole supply chain is being run by side deals. Spot prices are the least informative part. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: Kpler suspects Hormuz transit is being paid for. If so, 'ceasefire odds' are the wrong variable; the right one is who is collecting.

items.title: Claude Motion: Claude writes animations as code, exports MP4 (Team/Enterprise beta)
items.idea: Anthropic's Claude Motion turns reports, charts and walkthroughs into short animations; frames written purely in code with no video model, basic edits possible before MP4 export; beta on Team/Enterprise, off by default; invoked via '/motion'. Dashboards were the bigger enterprise shift this week.
items.angle: Code-as-video: deterministic, editable, cheap. Hits After Effects/motion freelancers and investor-deck workflows.
items.tweetA: Claude Motion writes each frame as code, not pixels. No video model, so you can edit the output with words. It's the first generative video that behaves like a spreadsheet. $ADBE should read this twice.
items.tweetB: Every analyst chart can now be a 20-second explainer without a designer. The cost of motion graphics just went to a few cents of tokens.

items.title: Dollar drives metals: DXY rally since January caused the gold/silver correction; August rebound reversed by a one-month dollar surge
items.idea: The 2025 dollar decline fueled the precious metals surge into January 2026; the sharp dollar rally since then drove the correction. August rebound (dollar drop) was halted by the dollar's surge over the past month. Same inverse relation to GSCI non-energy. Argument for gold standard reducing this volatility.
items.angle: Dollar heading for longest weekly advance since early 2025 (Apollo). Metals are a FX trade right now.
items.tweetA: The dollar is heading for its longest weekly win streak since early 2025. Metals have been trading as inverse DXY since January. Gold bugs waiting for fundamentals are fighting the wrong chart. $GLD $DXY
items.tweetB: If real yields are doing the work (5.2% 10-year) and the dollar is firm, gold's 'buy season' needs a dollar catalyst, not a geopolitical one.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Apollo Weekender
items.title: Weekender: Brent $104.72, 10Y ~5.24% (high 5.36%), 30Y >5.70%: the Treasury auctions were fine, the market is repricing the rent on money
items.idea: Stocks near highs because earnings (25% Q3 consensus, seven straight double-digit quarters) absorb $100 oil and 5%+ yields. 10Y sale was strong, 30Y serviceable, yet yields rose: a capital-scarcity repricing driven by real yields. Fed minutes hawkish; most officials see another hike likely by year-end; low-hire, low-fire. 'Monetary policy cannot build a substation.'
items.angle: Supply-side bottleneck (power, GPUs) means rate hikes are a blunt instrument. Real yield move = capital scarcity, not inflation.
items.tweetA: Auctions went fine and yields went up anyway. That isn't a supply problem, it's the price of capital rising because Washington, data centers, grids and fabs are all at the same window. You can't hike your way to more transformers.
items.tweetB: A 30-year over 5.70% with strong auction demand means buyers are willing to own it only at a higher price. That is a regime, not a wobble.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Apollo Weekender
items.title: Credit is discriminating before equities: Oracle CDS at record, Broadcom widening, CCC at multi-year wides; $166bn into money funds in one week
items.idea: Oracle CDS at record levels, Broadcom's widened sharply, CCC spreads at multi-year wides while IG spreads and VIX are calm. Broadcom seeking tens of billions of private debt; Oracle exploring off-balance-sheet structures; AI borrowing competes with Treasury supply. $166bn into MMFs in one week = optionality, not capitulation. S&P near records while a large share of members sit in correction.
items.angle: The AI buildout's funding stack is migrating from cash flow to private debt and SPVs. CDS is the early signal.
items.tweetA: Oracle CDS at a record, Broadcom widening, VIX asleep. Credit is pricing the cost of the buildout while equity prices the benefit. One of them is wrong by Q1. $ORCL $AVGO
items.tweetB: $166bn into money funds in a week and S&P near highs. That is not fear. It's investors holding cash with the intention of buying credit wides later.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Apollo Weekender
items.title: Hurricane Isaias shut in ~63% of Gulf crude production, and it was treated as a 'short-lived weather trade'
items.idea: Isaias shut in roughly 63% of Gulf crude output. In a normal year a short-lived weather trade; in this market with products stretched and diesel the inflation driver, even a temporary outage hits hard. Washington can lower the thermostat with headlines but cannot repair the furnace.
items.angle: 63% of Gulf production offline is a large number that barely moved the narrative. Physical tightness underlying.
items.tweetA: 63% of Gulf of Mexico crude production shut in by a hurricane and the market shrugged to $104. That is how tight everything already is, or how numb. $XOM $OXY
items.tweetB: Weather shut-in + Hormuz + diesel shortage. Three independent supply shocks stacked. The risk premium is not the news; the missing spare capacity is.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Apollo Weekender
items.title: France OATs stabilise but EUR/USD slides toward 1.1160; Brazil rallies on fiscal discipline prospects
items.idea: OATs stabilized after prior week's stress but the fiscal premium has migrated into EUR/USD (toward 1.1160). Brazil assets exploded higher on prospects of greater fiscal discipline: credibility commands a premium.
items.angle: Sovereign credibility is being priced through FX. France vs Brazil as a mirror trade.
items.tweetA: France pays for its fiscal credibility through the euro now. Brazil is getting paid for the promise of discipline. EM and DM sovereign stories have swapped places. $EWZ $FXE
items.tweetB: Dollar up, EUR/USD down, OATs wobbling.

items.title: 'The CEO's singular impact on the success or failure of AI': leadership can't be delegated
items.idea: McKinsey (Andy West, Sebastien Lacroix): there are aspects of the AI opportunity CEOs cannot hand off: raising the organization's ambition, re-architecting how it works, and resetting culture. Email body is a teaser only; the article has the data.
items.angle: Consultants framing AI as a CEO-owned transformation. Useful as read on how consulting is marketing the AI-capex payoff narrative. Charts inside likely.
items.tweetA: If AI success is mostly decided by the CEO's willingness to reorganize, then most of the enterprise AI spending is a bet on management quality, not model quality.
items.tweetB: McKinsey's pitch: AI fails for leadership reasons. Translation: the ROI gap is going to be blamed on org charts, not on the tech.

items.title: Gold and silver 'buy season' likely starts in November; B2Gold and Barrick highlighted
items.idea: Conversation on tricky current seasonality in precious metals and what would trigger a flip to 'buy season' in November; Lanci's variant view on US midterms; B2Gold (BTG) singled out for fundamentals plus chart at support. Author owns BTG and Barrick. Video content with minimal text.
items.angle: Seasonality framing lines up with TLT's mid-November bottom case: a shared late-year rotation thesis.
items.tweetA: TLT seasonality says low in mid-November. Gold seasonality says buy season starts in November. If both are right, a lot of people are going to be looking at the same date. $GLD $BTG
items.tweetB: Midterm outcomes as a gold variable: Lanci has a variant view. The dollar is the swing factor as per Bubble Bubble.

items.title: Jobless claims 197k, Atlanta Fed wage tracker 3.9% (back to pre-COVID trend), job switchers 4.7% vs stayers 3.4%
items.idea: Initial claims 197k (4-wk avg 198k); continuing 1.716mm vs 1.9mm most of last year. Atlanta Fed wage tracker 3.9% y/y; job switchers 4.7% (from 5%), stayers 3.4% (from 3.6%). NY Fed survey: better unemployment expectations and quit rate.
items.angle: Labor is not what's forcing the Fed; oil and real yields are. Wage tracker back to trend means no wage-price spiral.
items.tweetA: Claims at 197k, wages back to pre-COVID trend, quit-rate expectations improving. The labor market isn't the reason the Fed might hike again. Oil is. That's a very different kind of hike. $TLT
items.tweetB: Switchers 4.7%, stayers 3.4%: still a 130bp premium to move. Low-hire, low-fire has a price.

items.title: Used car wholesale prices -1.1% m/m in September as diesel at records and rates 'climbing rapidly' hit buyers
items.idea: Manheim: wholesale used-vehicle prices -1.1% m/m and -0.6% y/y; depreciation steeper than typical; first half of year showed more appreciation than usual despite fuel prices. Cites Middle East conflict, record diesel, rapidly climbing rates. Also container rates slightly lower: Shanghai-NY -2% w/w but >$10,000.
items.angle: Goods disinflation channel (used cars) offsets energy; container still >$10k per box.
items.tweetA: Used car prices -1.1% in a month and $10,000 containers. Goods deflation and shipping inflation in the same week. Core goods is getting squeezed from both sides.
items.tweetB: Higher rates are finally hitting the goods that financing built: autos. Used car wholesale is the earliest CPI leading indicator and it's rolling over.

items.title: August imports +4.3% m/m 'reflect the massive GenAI capex spend'; July revised up
items.idea: US imports rose 4.3% m/m in August (July revised up), attributed to GenAI capex equipment; exports +1.4% after -2.1%.
items.angle: AI capex is showing up in the trade deficit: the US is importing its buildout. Capex funded partly by foreign capital.
items.tweetA: Imports +4.3% in a month. AI servers and components are widening the trade deficit. The US is importing the buildout and borrowing the money from abroad to pay for it. That's a current account story.
items.tweetB: Capex boom = import boom = deficit widening = Treasury supply from overseas buyers.

items.title: Delta absorbs $6B fuel cost increase and still guides ~$4.5B pre-tax profit; premium revenue +18%
items.idea: Delta: expects ~$4.5B full-year pre-tax profit, absorbing a $6B fuel increase; main cabin unit revenue +17% on seats down low single digits; premium revenue +18% with double-digit unit revenue growth on 6% more seats. Air travel 'one of the best values'.
items.angle: Demand-side pricing power: airlines passing through a $6B fuel shock. K-shaped consumer, premium cabin.
items.tweetA: Delta ate a $6B fuel bill and still guides $4.5B in profit. Seats down, unit revenue up 17%. Capacity discipline plus premium demand is a margin machine. The K-shape is a cabin layout. $DAL
items.tweetB: Consumer confidence at 46.3 but premium seats are full. Asset owners vs non-owners, in aircraft form.

items.title: 'Too much natural gas': peak Lower 48 production ~113 Bcf/d is more than the market can absorb in 2027, driven by Permian associated gas
items.idea: Author believes Lower 48 peak production of ~113 Bcf/d is too high for 2027. Dry-gas producers have been disciplined; the problem is associated gas from Permian oil producers, driven by high oil prices. 2027 balance looks weak but he believes it's a temporary glut.
items.angle: High oil prices create gas oversupply through associated gas: $100 crude leads to a gas glut. Opposite of the usual energy complex correlation. LNG export timing is the pressure valve.
items.tweetA: $100 oil is quietly creating a natural gas glut. Permian associated gas doesn't care about Henry Hub, it comes with the oil. The oil bull case is the gas bear case. $EQT $AR $LNG
items.tweetB: 113 Bcf/d production vs a 2027 balance that doesn't clear. Gas producers disciplined, oil producers not. Capex discipline at the wrong commodity.
